claims.text: Hydride-derived Group IV-containing refractory powders may contain about 1.07 wt% oxygen if oxygen is not strictly controlled.
The hydride-derived powder microstructure is prone to brittle alpha-HCP precipitation during slow cooling or high-temperature exposure.
The proposed processing route uses SPS at 1300–1400 °C, 50 MPa, under vacuum below 10^-2 Pa, with a 2–5 minute dwell and immediate quenching.
A vacuum environment prevents oxygen uptake during SPS.
Rapid thermal cycling suppresses the thermodynamic driving force for alpha-HCP precipitation.
Rapid heating and short dwell times kinetically inhibit oxygen diffusion and thereby prevent oxide particles and HCP phases from forming at grain boundaries.
Raising the SPS temperature from 1200 °C to 1400 °C promotes reverse dissolution of Laves phases in CrMoNbWV.
Raising the SPS temperature to 1400 °C promotes reverse dissolution of oxides in CrMoNbWV.
A dwell of no more than five minutes prevents grain growth.
A short dwell limits oxygen diffusion and HCP-phase nucleation.
Rapid SPS retains a metastable solid-solution or BCC state instead of allowing transformation to brittle HCP phases.
Brittle HCP phases are thermodynamically favored at lower temperatures or at high oxygen content.
The proposed SPS treatment will produce residual porosity below 1%.
The proposed treatment will limit the alpha-HCP phase fraction to below 5%.
The resulting Group IV-containing alloy will have high-temperature compressive yield strength above 2700 MPa.
The proposed treatment will densify the alloy without catastrophic cracking.
A metastable BCC structure maximizes high-temperature yield strength through solid-solution and grain-boundary strengthening.
Conventional vacuum arc melting or slow sintering of hydride-derived powders typically causes oxygen uptake above 1.0 wt%, alpha-HCP and oxide precipitation, and catastrophic cracking.
An initial oxygen content below approximately 1.1 wt% is a critical threshold for avoiding irreversible oxide precipitation and brittle fracture.
High Zr/Hf content can intrinsically favor an HCP phase unless enough BCC-stabilizing elements are present.

contradictions.description: The boundary explicitly allows rapid SPS to fail by cracking when oxygen exceeds about 1.1 wt%, but the falsification rule treats cracking of the deliberately above-threshold 1.5 wt% sample as falsification. That result would instead be consistent with the stated boundary.

The structural mediator says rapid cycling suppresses the thermodynamic driving force for HCP precipitation, whereas the mechanism principally describes kinetic suppression of diffusion and nucleation. A faster thermal cycle can limit transformation kinetics but does not by itself remove the thermodynamic driving force.
